name: Chapter 7: Alternating Current
description: rms values, phasors, R, L, C in ac, series LCR, resonance, power factor, transformers and power transmission

cards.term: Main reason ac is preferred over dc for power supply?
cards.definition: Ac voltage can be easily and efficiently stepped up or down with transformers, and transmitted economically over long distances

cards.term: Form of the mains ac voltage?
cards.definition: A sinusoidal function of time: v = v_m sin ωt

cards.term: Everyday use of a special property of ac circuits, named by NCERT?
cards.definition: Tuning a radio: resonance in an LCR circuit

cards.term: Ac voltage v = v_m sin ωt across a pure resistor. Current?
cards.definition: \( i = i_m\sin\omega t,\quad i_m = \dfrac{v_m}{R} \): Ohm’s law holds for ac too

cards.term: Phase relation between v and i in a pure resistor?
cards.definition: In phase (phase difference 0): both peak and vanish together

cards.term: Average current over a full cycle? Is there still heating?
cards.definition: Average i = 0, but heating goes as i²R (always positive), so energy is dissipated

cards.term: Instantaneous power in a resistor and its average?
cards.definition: p = i_m²R sin²ωt; average \( \bar p = \tfrac12 i_m^2R \), because ⟨sin²ωt⟩ = ½

cards.term: Define rms current and rms voltage.
cards.definition: \( I = \dfrac{i_m}{\sqrt2} = 0.707\,i_m,\quad V = \dfrac{v_m}{\sqrt2} = 0.707\,v_m \)

cards.term: What does the rms current mean physically?
cards.definition: The dc that gives the same average heating in the same resistor

cards.term: Average power of ac in a resistor using rms values?
cards.definition: \( P = I^2R = IV = \dfrac{V^2}{R} \): same form as dc

cards.term: Household supply “220 V”: is that rms or peak? Peak value?
cards.definition: rms. Peak v_m = √2 × 220 ≈ 311 V

cards.term: Note: NCERT’s “Points to ponder” quotes 240 V for the room outlet. What do exams use?
cards.definition: Use the value given; NCERT’s examples use 220 V (India’s nominal supply is now 230 V). Peak of 240 V rms ≈ 340 V

cards.term: Teacher addition: what does an ac ammeter or voltmeter read? A dc moving-coil meter?
cards.definition: Ac meters (hot-wire type) read rms. A moving-coil dc meter reads the average = 0 and would not deflect on ac

cards.term: Teacher addition: mean value of ac over a half cycle?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{2i_m}{\pi} = 0.637\,i_m \) (over a full cycle it is 0)

cards.term: Teacher addition: rms value of a general periodic current?
cards.definition: Square root of the mean of i² over a period. The 1/√2 factor is only for a sinusoid

cards.term: A 100 W, 220 V bulb (Example 7.1)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 7.1 · bulb

Find the missing step.

Bulb rated 100 W, 220 V. Find R, peak voltage and rms current.
  1. ?
  2. Peak voltage v_m = √2 V = 311 V
  3. I = P/V = 100/220 = 0.454 A
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 7.1 · bulb

Find the missing step.

Bulb rated 100 W, 220 V. Find R, peak voltage and rms current.
  1. R = V²/P = 220²/100 = 484 Ω
  2. Peak voltage v_m = √2 V = 311 V
  3. I = P/V = 100/220 = 0.454 A

cards.term: Trap: resistance of a 100 W, 220 V bulb when operated on 110 V?
cards.definition: R stays 484 Ω. Power drops to V²/R = 110²/484 = 25 W (quarter)

cards.term: What is a phasor?
cards.definition: A vector rotating about the origin with angular speed ω; its length is the amplitude and its vertical component is the instantaneous value

cards.term: Phasor diagram of a resistor: angle between V and I phasors?
cards.definition: 0: they point along the same line at all times

cards.term: Are voltage and current in ac really vectors?
cards.definition: No: they are scalars; phasors are only a device so harmonic quantities add by the vector addition rule

cards.term: Why use phasors?
cards.definition: To show phase relations between v and i and to add voltages across R, L, C easily

cards.term: Trap: how must voltages across R and C in series be added?
cards.definition: As phasors: \( V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + V_C^2} \), not V_R + V_C, because they are 90° out of phase

cards.term: Pure inductor, v = v_m sin ωt. Current?
cards.definition: \( i = i_m\sin(\omega t - \pi/2),\quad i_m = \dfrac{v_m}{\omega L} \)

cards.term: Derive the current in a pure inductor.
cards.definition: v = L di/dt → di/dt = (v_m/L) sin ωt. Integrate: i = −(v_m/ωL) cos ωt (integration constant 0 as no dc component) = i_m sin(ωt − π/2)

cards.term: Inductive reactance: formula, unit, dependence?
cards.definition: \( X_L = \omega L = 2\pi\nu L \); ohm; ∝ frequency and ∝ L. Zero for dc

cards.term: Phase relation in a pure inductor?
cards.definition: Current lags the voltage by π/2 (one quarter cycle)

cards.term: Average power absorbed by a pure inductor over a cycle?
cards.definition: Zero: p = −½ i_m v_m sin 2ωt averages to 0; energy is stored and returned

cards.term: Why does an inductor pass low frequencies more easily?
cards.definition: X_L = 2πνL is small for small ν; for dc X_L = 0

cards.term: Reactance and current in an inductor (Example 7.2)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 7.2 · pure inductor

Find the missing step.

25.0 mH inductor on a 220 V, 50 Hz source. Find X_L and rms current.
  1. X_L = 2πνL = 2 × 3.14 × 50 × 25 × 10⁻³
  2. ?
  3. I = V/X_L = 220/7.85 ≈ 28 A
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 7.2 · pure inductor

Find the missing step.

25.0 mH inductor on a 220 V, 50 Hz source. Find X_L and rms current.
  1. X_L = 2πνL = 2 × 3.14 × 50 × 25 × 10⁻³
  2. X_L = 7.85 Ω
  3. I = V/X_L = 220/7.85 ≈ 28 A

cards.term: Example 7.5: iron rod pushed into a coil in series with a bulb on ac. Bulb glow?
cards.definition: Decreases: L rises (μᵣ), so X_L rises and more of the supply voltage falls across the coil

cards.term: Teacher addition: choke coil?
cards.definition: An inductor used to reduce ac current without wasting power, unlike a series resistor (which dissipates I²R); its power factor is nearly zero

cards.term: Does a capacitor pass dc? Ac?
cards.definition: dc: current only during charging, then zero. Ac: it charges and discharges every half cycle, so current flows (limited)

cards.term: Capacitor, v = v_m sin ωt. Current?
cards.definition: \( i = i_m\sin(\omega t + \pi/2),\quad i_m = \omega C v_m \)

cards.term: Derive the current in a capacitor.
cards.definition: q = Cv = Cv_m sin ωt; i = dq/dt = ωCv_m cos ωt = ωCv_m sin(ωt + π/2)

cards.term: Capacitive reactance: formula, unit, dependence?
cards.definition: \( X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\nu C} \); ohm; inversely proportional to ν and C. Infinite for dc

cards.term: Phase relation in a pure capacitor?
cards.definition: Current leads the voltage by π/2

cards.term: Average power absorbed by a pure capacitor?
cards.definition: Zero over a cycle: p = ½ i_m v_m sin 2ωt averages to 0

cards.term: Mnemonic for phase in L and C?
cards.definition: “CIVIL”: in a C the I leads V; in an L the V leads I

cards.term: Example 7.3: lamp in series with a capacitor: dc source, then ac source; C reduced?
cards.definition: dc: lamp does not glow (no steady current). Ac: lamp glows; smaller C → larger X_C → dimmer

cards.term: Reactance and current in a capacitor (Example 7.4)
cards.definition: X_C = 212 Ω, I = 1.04 A, i_m = 1.47 A; current doubles

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 7.4 · capacitor

Find the missing step.

15.0 μF capacitor on 220 V, 50 Hz. Find X_C, rms and peak current. What if ν doubles?
  1. X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 15 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 212 Ω
  2. ?
  3. Peak i_m = √2 I = 1.47 A, leading V by π/2
  4. ν doubled: X_C halves → current doubles
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 7.4 · capacitor

Find the missing step.

15.0 μF capacitor on 220 V, 50 Hz. Find X_C, rms and peak current. What if ν doubles?
  1. X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 15 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 212 Ω
  2. I = V/X_C = 220/212 = 1.04 A
  3. Peak i_m = √2 I = 1.47 A, leading V by π/2
  4. ν doubled: X_C halves → current doubles

cards.term: Pure R, L and C in ac
cards.definition: Resistor: R; i in phase with v; power dissipated; Inductor: X_L = ωL; i lags v by π/2; P = 0; Capacitor: X_C = 1/ωC; i leads v by π/2; P = 0; Effect of raising ν: R same; X_L up; X_C down

cards.term: Loop equation of a series LCR circuit?
cards.definition: \( L\dfrac{di}{dt} + iR + \dfrac{q}{C} = v \)

cards.term: In a series LCR circuit, what is common to R, L and C?
cards.definition: The current (same amplitude and phase). Voltages differ in phase

cards.term: Phases of V_R, V_L, V_C relative to I?
cards.definition: V_R in phase with I; V_L leads I by π/2; V_C lags I by π/2

cards.term: Amplitudes of the three voltages?
cards.definition: v_Rm = i_m R, v_Lm = i_m X_L, v_Cm = i_m X_C

cards.term: Why can V_L and V_C be combined into one phasor?
cards.definition: They lie along the same line in opposite directions: net magnitude |v_Cm − v_Lm|

cards.term: Impedance of a series LCR circuit?
cards.definition: \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2},\quad i_m = \dfrac{v_m}{Z} \)

cards.term: Phase angle φ of the current in a series LCR circuit (i = i_m sin(ωt + φ))?
cards.definition: \( \tan\phi = \dfrac{X_C - X_L}{R} \)

cards.term: If X_C > X_L: nature of circuit, sign of φ, current?
cards.definition: Predominantly capacitive φ positive current leads the source voltage

cards.term: If X_L > X_C: nature of circuit, sign of φ, current?
cards.definition: Predominantly inductive φ negative current lags the source voltage

cards.term: Trap: with φ defined as “angle of current relative to voltage”, sign of φ?
cards.definition:
NCERT uses \( \tan\phi = \dfrac{X_C - X_L}{R} \) (angle of i).
Many books define φ = angle of v, giving X_L − X_C. Check the definition in the question

cards.term: Teacher addition: Z for an RL circuit and an RC circuit?
cards.definition: RL: \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} \), current lags. RC: \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2} \), current leads

cards.term: Limitation of the phasor method?
cards.definition: Gives only the steady-state solution (no initial conditions); the transient part dies out after some time

cards.term: Voltages in an RC circuit (Example 7.6)
cards.definition: I = 0.755 A, V_R = 151 V, V_C = 160.3 V, quadrature sum = 220 V

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 7.6 · RC series

Find the missing step.

200 Ω resistor and 15.0 μF capacitor in series on 220 V, 50 Hz. Find I and the voltage across each. Why do the two voltages add to more than 220 V?
  1. X_C = 212.3 Ω; Z = √(200² + 212.3²) ≈ 291.7 Ω
  2. I = V/Z = 220/291.7 = 0.755 A
  3. V_R = IR = 151 V, V_C = IX_C = 160.3 V (sum 311 V > 220 V)
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 7.6 · RC series

Find the missing step.

200 Ω resistor and 15.0 μF capacitor in series on 220 V, 50 Hz. Find I and the voltage across each. Why do the two voltages add to more than 220 V?
  1. X_C = 212.3 Ω; Z = √(200² + 212.3²) ≈ 291.7 Ω
  2. I = V/Z = 220/291.7 = 0.755 A
  3. V_R = IR = 151 V, V_C = IX_C = 160.3 V (sum 311 V > 220 V)
  4. They are 90° out of phase: V = √(V_R² + V_C²) = 220 V ✓

cards.term: Resonance in a series LCR circuit: condition and frequency?
cards.definition: X_L = X_C → \( \omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},\ \nu_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} \)

cards.term: What happens at resonance?
cards.definition: Z is minimum (Z = R) current is maximum, \( i_m = v_m/R \) φ = 0 (current in phase with v) V_L and V_C cancel

cards.term: Effect of increasing R on the resonance curve?
cards.definition: Peak height falls (i_m = v_m/R) and the curve gets broader (less sharp). R = 100 Ω gives twice the peak of R = 200 Ω

cards.term: Can resonance occur in an RL or RC circuit? Why?
cards.definition: No: needs both L and C so that V_L and V_C can cancel

cards.term: Mechanical analogy for resonance?
cards.definition: A child on a swing pushed at its natural frequency: amplitude grows large

cards.term: How does a radio tune to a station?
cards.definition: Vary C so that ω₀ = 1/√LC matches the station’s frequency: current at that frequency is maximum

cards.term: Example 7.10: how does an airport metal detector work?
cards.definition: Walk-through coil + capacitor tuned to resonance; metal changes L, so impedance and current change, triggering the alarm

cards.term: Teacher addition: quality factor Q of a series LCR circuit?
cards.definition: \( Q = \dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0 CR} = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}} \): measures the sharpness of resonance (dimensionless)

cards.term: Teacher addition: bandwidth and its link to Q?
cards.definition: Half-power bandwidth \( \Delta\omega = \dfrac{R}{L} = \dfrac{\omega_0}{Q} \): higher Q → narrower, sharper resonance

cards.term: Teacher addition: voltage across L or C at resonance compared with the source?
cards.definition: V_L = V_C = Q × V, which can be far larger than the source voltage (while V_L and V_C cancel each other)

cards.term: Average power in a series LCR circuit?
cards.definition: \( P = VI\cos\phi = I^2Z\cos\phi \); cos φ = power factor = R/Z

cards.term: Derive P = VI cos φ.
cards.definition: p = vi = ½ v_m i_m [cos φ − cos(2ωt + φ)]; the second term averages to 0, so P = ½ v_m i_m cos φ = V I cos φ

cards.term: Power factor of a purely resistive circuit? Power?
cards.definition: cos φ = 1: maximum power dissipation

cards.term: Power factor and average power of a pure L or pure C?
cards.definition: φ = π/2 → cos φ = 0, no power, though current flows: wattless current

cards.term: In an LCR circuit, in which element is power dissipated?
cards.definition: Only in the resistor: P = I²R

cards.term: Power and power factor at resonance?
cards.definition: cos φ = 1 and P = I²R = V²/R, the maximum

cards.term: Example 7.7: why does a low power factor cause large transmission loss?
cards.definition: P = IV cos φ: for fixed P and V, small cos φ needs larger I, so the I²R loss in the lines rises

cards.term: How is the power factor improved?
cards.definition: Connect a suitable capacitor in parallel: its leading wattless current cancels the lagging wattless component I_q

cards.term: Power component and wattless component of current?
cards.definition: I_p = I cos φ (along V, gives power). I_q = I sin φ (⊥ V, wattless)

cards.term: Series LCR calculation (Example 7.8)
cards.definition: Z = 5 Ω, φ = −53.1°, P = 4800 W, power factor 0.6

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 7.8 · LCR numbers

Find the missing step.

v_m = 283 V, ν = 50 Hz, R = 3 Ω, L = 25.48 mH, C = 796 μF in series. Find Z, φ, P and power factor.
  1. X_L = 2πνL = 8 Ω, X_C = 1/2πνC = 4 Ω
  2. Z = √(3² + (8 − 4)²) = 5 Ω
  3. ?
  4. I = 283/(√2 × 5) = 40 A; P = I²R = 4800 W; cos φ = 0.6
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 7.8 · LCR numbers

Find the missing step.

v_m = 283 V, ν = 50 Hz, R = 3 Ω, L = 25.48 mH, C = 796 μF in series. Find Z, φ, P and power factor.
  1. X_L = 2πνL = 8 Ω, X_C = 1/2πνC = 4 Ω
  2. Z = √(3² + (8 − 4)²) = 5 Ω
  3. tan φ = (X_C − X_L)/R = −4/3 → φ = −53.1° (current lags)
  4. I = 283/(√2 × 5) = 40 A; P = I²R = 4800 W; cos φ = 0.6

cards.term: Resonance of the LCR circuit (Example 7.9)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 7.9 · resonance

Find the missing step.

Same circuit, frequency now variable. Find ν₀, and Z, I, P at resonance.
  1. ?
  2. ν₀ = ω₀/2π = 35.4 Hz
  3. Z = R = 3 Ω; I = (283/√2)/3 = 66.7 A
  4. P = I²R = 13.35 kW (more than at 50 Hz)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 7.9 · resonance

Find the missing step.

Same circuit, frequency now variable. Find ν₀, and Z, I, P at resonance.
  1. ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(25.48 × 10⁻³ × 796 × 10⁻⁶) = 222.1 rad/s
  2. ν₀ = ω₀/2π = 35.4 Hz
  3. Z = R = 3 Ω; I = (283/√2)/3 = 66.7 A
  4. P = I²R = 13.35 kW (more than at 50 Hz)

cards.term: Teacher addition: a series LCR at 50 Hz has X_L = X_C. What is I?
cards.definition: V/R (resonance at 50 Hz), and V_R = V (whole source across R)

cards.term: Principle and parts of a transformer?
cards.definition: Mutual induction. Primary (N_p turns) and secondary (N_s turns) on a soft-iron core

cards.term: Voltage ratio of an ideal transformer?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} \)

cards.term: Current ratio of an ideal transformer?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{I_s}{I_p} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s} = \dfrac{V_p}{V_s} \) (from V_pI_p = V_sI_s)

cards.term: Step-up vs step-down transformer?
cards.definition: Step-up: N_s > N_p, V rises, I falls. Step-down: N_s < N_p, V falls, I rises

cards.term: Does a step-up transformer violate energy conservation?
cards.definition: No: voltage rises but current falls in the same ratio; power in = power out (ideal)

cards.term: Assumptions behind V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p?
cards.definition: Negligible primary resistance and current all flux links both coils small secondary current

cards.term: Why is e_p = v_p in an ideal transformer?
cards.definition: Else the primary current would be infinite (zero resistance); the back emf equals the applied voltage

cards.term: Example: primary 100 turns, secondary 200 turns, 220 V at 10 A input. Output?
cards.definition: 440 V at 5.0 A

cards.term: Efficiency of a transformer?
cards.definition: \( \eta = \dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} = \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_pI_p} \); well-designed ones exceed 95%

cards.term: List the four energy losses in a real transformer and remedy for each.
cards.definition: (i) Flux leakage: wind coils over one another. (ii) Resistance of windings (I²R): thick wire. (iii) Eddy currents: laminated core. (iv) Hysteresis: low-loss soft magnetic material

cards.term: Why is the core laminated?
cards.definition: Insulated thin sheets break up eddy current loops in the iron, reducing heating

cards.term: Why is transmission done at high voltage?
cards.definition: For fixed power P = VI, high V means small I, so the I²R loss in the lines is small

cards.term: Steps in power transmission, per NCERT?
cards.definition: Generator voltage stepped up → long-distance lines → area sub-station steps down → distribution sub-stations and poles → about 240 V at homes

cards.term: Teacher addition: power loss in a line of resistance R carrying P at voltage V?
cards.definition: \( P_{loss} = I^2R = \dfrac{P^2R}{V^2} \): raising V tenfold cuts loss 100×

cards.term: Teacher addition: can a transformer work on dc? Why?
cards.definition: No: needs changing flux; a steady primary current gives no induced secondary emf

cards.term: Teacher addition: does a transformer change the frequency?
cards.definition: No: output has the same frequency as the input

cards.term: Rating of an ac appliance (e.g. 60 W)?
cards.definition: Refers to average power (rms based)

cards.term: Can power consumed in an ac circuit be negative on average?
cards.definition: No: the average power P = VI cos φ is never negative (instantaneous power in L and C can be)

cards.term: How is the ac ampere defined?
cards.definition: 1 A rms = the alternating current producing the same average heating as 1 A dc (the force between wires averages to zero for ac)

cards.term: Generator vs motor?
cards.definition: Generator: mechanical → electrical. Motor: electrical → mechanical. Both just transform energy

cards.term: Where are the losses in an ac circuit?
cards.definition: Only in resistive elements; pure L and C have none

cards.term: Why does the power factor matter?
cards.definition: It measures how close the circuit is to using the maximum power for the given V and I

cards.term: Exercise 7.3: 44 mH inductor on 220 V, 50 Hz. rms current?
Exercise 7.4: 60 μF capacitor on 110 V, 60 Hz. rms current?

cards.term: Exercise 7.6: charged 30 μF capacitor joined to a 27 mH inductor. Angular frequency of free oscillations?
Exercise 7.7: R = 20 Ω, L = 1.5 H, C = 35 μF, 200 V supply at the natural frequency. Average power?
cards.definition: At resonance Z = R, so P = V²/R = 200²/20 = 2000 W

cards.term: Resonating series LCR circuit (Exercise 7.8)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 7.8 · resonating LCR

Find the missing step.

L = 5.0 H, C = 80 μF, R = 40 Ω, 230 V source. (a) ω₀ (b) Z and current amplitude (c) rms voltage across each element.
  1. ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(5 × 80 × 10⁻⁶) = 50 rad/s
  2. Z = R = 40 Ω; i_m = √2 × 230/40 = 8.1 A
  3. I_rms = 230/40 = 5.75 A; X_L = X_C = 250 Ω
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 7.8 · resonating LCR

Find the missing step.

L = 5.0 H, C = 80 μF, R = 40 Ω, 230 V source. (a) ω₀ (b) Z and current amplitude (c) rms voltage across each element.
  1. ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(5 × 80 × 10⁻⁶) = 50 rad/s
  2. Z = R = 40 Ω; i_m = √2 × 230/40 = 8.1 A
  3. I_rms = 230/40 = 5.75 A; X_L = X_C = 250 Ω
  4. V_L = V_C = 5.75 × 250 = 1437.5 V, V_R = 230 V; V_L − V_C = 0

cards.term: Exercise 7.8: how can V_L = 1437.5 V exist with a 230 V source?
cards.definition: V_L and V_C are 180° out of phase and cancel exactly; each is Q times the source (Q = 6.25)

cards.term: Chapter 7 formula sheet
cards.definition: rms current, voltage: I = i_m/√2, V = v_m/√2; Average power (resistor): P = I²R = IV; Inductive reactance: X_L = ωL; Capacitive reactance: X_C = 1/ωC; Impedance (LCR): Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²); Phase angle: tan φ = (X_C − X_L)/R; Resonant frequency: ω₀ = 1/√LC; Average power: P = VI cos φ; Quality factor: Q = ω₀L/R = 1/ω₀CR; Transformer: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p = I_p/I_s

Summary

Formula?

rms current, voltageI = i_m/√2, V = v_m/√2
Average power (resistor)P = I²R = IV
Inductive reactanceX_L = ωL
Capacitive reactanceX_C = 1/ωC
Impedance (LCR)Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²)
Phase angletan φ = (X_C − X_L)/R
Resonant frequencyω₀ = 1/√LC
Average powerP = VI cos φ
Quality factorQ = ω₀L/R = 1/ω₀CR
TransformerV_s/V_p = N_s/N_p = I_p/I_s
